title: Negative feelings
subtitle: antipathy, aversion, loathe, distraught
summary: Name dislike precisely - from mild irritation to loathing and abhorrence - and describe unpleasant people and deep unhappiness.

lesson.heading: Antipathy and aversion
lesson.text: **Antipathy** is a feeling of strong, often active, dislike or opposition towards something or someone. An **aversion** is a feeling of intense dislike or an unwillingness to do something; it is often used in the phrase **have** or **feel an aversion to**. Your **pet aversion** is the thing you dislike most of all.

examples.text: **Antipathy** towards the government increased during the economic crisis.
I felt an instant **aversion to** the new manager.
Arrogance has always been my **pet aversion**.
I have a strong **aversion to** people who always want to be the centre of attention.

lesson.heading: Averse to
lesson.text: **Averse to** means opposed to, and it is usually used with **not**. Saying you are **not averse to** something is a mild, slightly humorous way of saying you rather enjoy it.

examples.text: I'm **not averse to** a good night out.
examples.note: = I enjoy a good night out

examples.text: I am **not averse to** a vegetarian diet. I've just never tried it.
She is **averse to** any kind of change in the office.

lesson.heading: Nouns, adjectives and verbs of dislike
rows: a feeling of being extremely upset or worried
a feeling of being very worried or frightened

lesson.heading: Using them
lesson.text: Notice the strength: **irritation** is only annoyance, but **loathing** is intense hatred and **abhorrence** is intense disgust. The **-ing** form describes the thing that causes the feeling; the **-ed** form describes the person experiencing it.

examples.text: I just **loathe** people who tell lies.

examples.note: She abhors injustice, wherever it occurs.

examples.text: There was a **scornful** note in his voice.
The advance of the enemy troops across the river was an **alarming** development, and we were all **alarmed**.

lesson.heading: Adjectives with negative connotations
rows: showing a rude lack of interest in others
too eager to tell others what to do
displaying wealth or possessions in a vulgar way
too formal, and showing that you think you are more important than others
trying to appear more serious or important than you are
not taking care in the way you work (informal)
changing your feelings suddenly without reason

lesson.heading: Those adjectives in sentences
lesson.text: These are all strong criticisms, so choose the exact one. **Ostentatious** is about showing off money; **pretentious** is about showing off taste or intelligence; **pompous** is about self-importance.

examples.text: He makes very **ostentatious** displays of his wealth, with big, flashy cars and designer clothes.
She boasts about reading philosophy books - she's so **pretentious**.
She's become very **pompous** since she was elected to Parliament.
The customs officer was such an **obnoxious** man.

lesson.heading: Being extremely unhappy
rows: sad, alone and not cared for

lesson.text: The -ing adjective describes the cause (the news was distressing); the -ed adjective describes the person (I felt distressed).

exercises.prompt: I have a strong ___ to people who always want to be the centre of attention.
exercises.explanation: An aversion is a feeling of intense dislike; you have an aversion to something.

exercises.prompt: He always ___ our amateur theatrical productions - he has no respect for them at all.
exercises.explanation: To scorn something is to show a lack of respect for it.

exercises.prompt: She ___ injustice, wherever it occurs.
exercises.explanation: To abhor something is to feel intense disgust at it.

exercises.prompt: I've just never tried a vegetarian diet - but I am not ___ to it.
exercises.explanation: Averse to means opposed to, and is usually used with not.

exercises.prompt: His attitude was very ___.
exercises.explanation: The -ing form describes the cause of the feeling; you could also say I was irritated by his attitude.

exercises.prompt: We were all ___ when we heard the news.
exercises.explanation: The -ed form describes the person experiencing the feeling.

exercises.prompt: The palace was very ___, with gold ceilings and marble statues everywhere.
exercises.explanation: Ostentatious means displaying wealth or possessions in a vulgar way.

exercises.prompt: One of my friends is a bit ___; he has a new girlfriend every week!
exercises.explanation: A fickle person changes their feelings suddenly without reason.

exercises.prompt: She thinks I'm ___ because I like opera, but I like pop music too.
exercises.hint: (trying to seem more important than you are)
exercises.explanation: A pretentious person tries to appear more serious or important than they are.

exercises.prompt: The lawyers were very ___ when they were dealing with the complicated will.
exercises.explanation: Nit-picking means too concerned about unimportant details.

exercises.prompt: The decorators were very ___ and didn't paint the kitchen properly.
exercises.explanation: Sloppy means not taking care in the way you work.

exercises.prompt: He's an ___ person; absolutely nobody thinks he's nice.
exercises.explanation: An obnoxious person is unpleasant and rude.

exercises.prompt: The receptionist was very ___ with me, and didn't seem to take me seriously.
exercises.explanation: Offhand means showing a rude lack of interest in others.

exercises.prompt: The Minister made a very ___ speech, and seemed full of his own importance.
exercises.explanation: Pompous means too formal and showing that you think you are more important than other people.

exercises.prompt: The man at the museum was very ___, telling us to be quiet and not to touch the exhibits.
exercises.explanation: An officious person is too eager to tell others what to do.

exercises.prompt: Match the beginnings and endings of these sentences.

pairs.left: He was looking a bit down
pairs.right: so I offered to buy him a coffee.
by the death of so many good friends.

pairs.left: She was quite a miserable person
pairs.right: who rarely laughed or enjoyed herself.

exercises.prompt: If you are distressed by a piece of news, you are ___.
exercises.explanation: Distress is a feeling of being extremely upset or worried.

exercises.prompt: If someone feels antipathy towards another person, they ___.
exercises.explanation: Antipathy is a feeling of strong, often active, dislike or opposition.

exercises.prompt: If someone irritates you, you feel ___.
exercises.explanation: Irritation is a feeling of being annoyed - much weaker than loathing or abhorrence.

exercises.statement: If you find something loathsome, you feel intense hatred towards it.
exercises.explanation: Correct - loathing is intense hatred, and the verb is loathe.

exercises.prompt: Does each word describe an unpleasant person or an unhappy person?
Put this sentence in order.
exercises.answer: I felt an instant aversion to the new manager
exercises.explanation: You feel or have an aversion to someone or something.
